geometric:cool: You want the circle to be a circle and the reasoning to stay visible, like a Bauhaus preliminary exercise that somehow ended up on a bank's letterhead.
You pick like a Vignelli associate in 1972, everything set with compass and rule and a quiet contempt for anything decided by hand.
geometric:warm: You keep reaching for Renner's compass and then asking it to be friendly, which is the argument Futura has lost with every children's book art director since 1930.
Your picks want Bauhaus geometry with a fire lit inside it, the way Dessau looks in photographs taken late in the afternoon rather than in the catalogue.
geometric:loud: You take the circle and the bar and then turn the volume up, which is what the poster shops of 1970s Milan did once the Swiss stopped watching.
You are using geometry as percussion, closer to a Neville Brody spread than to anything Herbert Bayer would sign, and you seem entirely comfortable there.
geometric:refined: You are running Renner through a fashion house, the circles kept pure and the tone kept expensive, the way Avant Garde looked before everyone abused the ligatures.
You want geometry with manners: Kabel's discipline on a magazine's margins, and the assumption that your reader will notice the sidebearings.
geometric:forward: You are shopping the aisle every space agency mockup shops in, though your circles are drawn better than theirs and you know which decade you are quoting.
Your picks read as a Bauhaus alphabet that received a firmware update, the geometry kept intact while everything around it starts behaving like an interface.
neogrotesque:cool: You are a Haas employee in 1957 with a scalpel and a deadline, and you would remove one more thing from this if the client allowed it.
Nothing in your votes wants to be noticed, which is the whole neo-grotesque proposition, a face that delivers the timetable and declines to sign it.
neogrotesque:warm: You want Helvetica to be kind to you, which is a request Miedinger never once entertained, and your picks keep going over his head about it.
You are the person who defends Univers at dinner by talking about the humanist part of its ancestry rather than the Swiss part everyone else means.
neogrotesque:loud: You set Swiss neutrality at four hundred point and let it shout, the trick every hardcore record sleeve borrowed from annual reports it had never read.
Your picks want a Vignelli signage system played through a stadium, neutral letters doing work that no neutral letter was ever drawn to do.
neogrotesque:refined: You edit like a mid-century art director who trusts a grid more than a photograph, and who would rather lose the picture than lose the alignment.
You want the anonymity to read as luxury, the move every fashion house made in 2016 when logos went flat and everyone pretended it was new.
neogrotesque:forward: You are the Swiss rationalist who bought a synthesizer, keeping the grid and the neutrality while the whole thing gets tooled like a machined part.
Your picks want Univers to be operating-system furniture, legible at four in the morning on a screen nobody is especially proud of owning.
grotesque:cool: The jobbing grotesque was cut for tram tickets and tax notices, and the indifference that came with that work is what you keep siding with.
Akzidenz spent sixty years being tidied into consistency, and you would plainly rather have it from before, since irregularity reads as evidence and evenness reads as a committee.
grotesque:warm: You like the nineteenth-century jobbing grotesque the way people like a worn tool, and your picks keep the small irregularities Monotype spent decades sanding off.
You are drawn to Franklin Gothic in a newspaper you read as a child, nostalgia arriving through a face that was drawn with no interest in nostalgia.
grotesque:loud: You want the grotesque that ends up in a doorway on a fly-posted bill, cut for prices and boxing matches rather than for identity systems.
You are shopping at the end of the grotesque's catalogue where letters got big because metal that size was unaffordable, and subtlety cost extra.
grotesque:refined: You are the art director who takes Benton's Franklin Gothic for a masthead and then sets the rest of the page in something that will never argue with it.
You want the industrial grotesque with its collar buttoned: ATF bones on an editorial margin, and spacing that has been fought over at least twice.
grotesque:forward: You are pulling a nineteenth-century jobbing face into a future it was not invited to, keeping the closed apertures and losing every trace of the pressman.
Your picks read as Akzidenz redrawn by someone building an interface for a vehicle, industrial bones with the ink squeeze engineered away.
humanist-sans:cool: Somewhere in these votes a person's handwriting survives, and you have put it to work labelling things rather than being liked.
Hans Meier drew Syntax off a Renaissance roman and then sent it out to caption machine parts, which is more or less the errand you have in mind.
humanist-sans:warm: Your picks have Edward Johnston's broad nib behind them, which is why they feel like a face someone drew rather than a face someone specified.
You want the sans that still remembers handwriting, the Gill Sans argument minus Gill himself, whose biography most people now decline to discuss.
humanist-sans:loud: You take a calligraphic sans and make it lean on you, which is what Spiekermann's Meta did to every startup that mistook it for something polite.
You want the pen strokes visible and the volume high, closer to a festival poster in Amsterdam than to the wayfinding manual these shapes came from.
humanist-sans:refined: You are setting a literary journal in Scala Sans, humanist proportions kept intact, and you will move the folio three millimetres until it sits right.
You want a sans with Renaissance proportions and a magazine's manners, the Frutiger idea taken indoors and given considerably better paper.
humanist-sans:forward: You keep the calligraphic skeleton and send it forward, which is the move behind every variable interface face released since 2018, and behind most of the bad ones.
You want Johnston's underground alphabet running on a display that did not exist when Johnston drew it, with warmth retained as a system requirement.
flared:cool: Zapf argued that Optima was a serif face without serifs, and you have taken him at his word and filed the result under instruments.
Hospital wayfinding is drawn in exactly this key, letters given just enough shape to look human and not one degree more, and that is where this set settles.
flared:warm: You are living inside Optima, which Zapf sketched from grave slabs in Santa Croce onto a banknote, stems breathing outward, letters carved rather than assembled.
Your picks want Wolpe's Albertus, cut for the City of London's street signs and photographed constantly by people who never learn its name.
flared:loud: You want Albertus doing the work it does on horror paperbacks and Portmeirion village signs, incised warmth turned into something faintly threatening.
You take a chiselled sans and push it until the flares read as claws, closer to a 1970s film title than to any war memorial.
flared:refined: You are the person who specifies Optima for a fashion house and gets away with it, which takes better spacing judgment than most people bring.
You want inscriptional dignity without the serifs, Zapf's answer to the Roman capital, set with the margins of an exhibition catalogue.
flared:forward: You want the carved stem to survive the screen, Optima's swelling kept as a signal rather than as a memory of a stonecutter's chisel.
Your picks read as lapidary lettering issued by an institution that does not exist yet and has already settled its identity guidelines.
wedge:cool: A triangle survives reduction and a bracketed serif does not, which is the entire case for the wedge, and it is the only part of the case your votes care about.
This is what happens when a technical documentation team reads one book about Roman inscriptions and keeps only the load-bearing part of it.
wedge:warm: Your picks sit where the chisel meets the pen, which is where Meridien lives, and you appear to want the paper it was printed on too.
You like a serif that admits it was cut rather than drawn, the way stone lettering in a country church admits the mason had a bad afternoon.
wedge:loud: You want Friz Quadrata doing what it did to a thousand heavy metal sleeves, the wedge sharpened until it stops reading as a serif at all.
Your picks take an incised face and make it aggressive, closer to a fight poster than to the Roman inscription these shapes were stolen from.
wedge:refined: You are setting a museum's wall text, Trajan's proportions with a wedge instead of a bracket, and nothing on that wall competing with the object.
You want the authority of carved capitals in a face that also has to hold a paragraph, the exact problem Meridien was drawn to solve.
wedge:forward: You keep the chisel and lose the century, incised serifs treated as engineering rather than as heritage, which is how science fiction title cards get made.
Your picks read as inscriptional lettering for a facility with no visitors, sharp and institutional, confident that legibility outlives style.
humanist-serif:cool: Five centuries of typographers have called Jenson's roman beautiful, and your votes file it under solved, which is a colder compliment and probably the one Jenson wanted.
Critical editions get set like this, humanist bones doing the reading and no flourish anywhere a proofreader could mistake for an opinion.
humanist-serif:warm: You are in Venice in 1470 with the ink still wet, choosing the slanted bar on the e and everything warm that arrives with it.
Your picks want Bruce Rogers' Centaur on decent paper, the letters that made typographers believe the Renaissance had already solved this problem.
humanist-serif:loud: You take a Venetian face and print it too heavily on purpose, closer to a fanzine's photocopier than to anything Nicolas Jenson pulled off a press.
You want humanist warmth with its voice raised, Bembo dragged onto a poster where nobody in the room expected to find it.
humanist-serif:refined: You are the person who reads the colophon, and your picks say Bembo with wide margins, plus an argument about the ampersand nobody asked to hear.
You want the Aldine page, generous leading over Venetian proportions, set for a reader you fully expect to stay for eight hundred pages.
humanist-serif:forward: You keep Jenson's calligraphic angle and put it somewhere new, which is what every screen-first text face has quietly attempted since Georgia shipped.
Your picks want a Renaissance skeleton rendered by a machine that has never seen paper, warmth retained as a deliberate engineering decision.
transitional:cool: There is a reason contracts and prayer books ended up in the same eighteenth-century roman, and your votes have arrived at it from the contract side.
As far as these votes are concerned, every argument about type since 1760 has been decoration on an answer the eighteenth century already published.
transitional:warm: You are reading Baskerville's own specimen and enjoying his vanity, wove paper, hot-pressed sheets, and letters that look lit from behind.
Your picks want a face from the Enlightenment that still sounds like a person talking, Bell or Fournier rather than the colder end of that shelf.
transitional:loud: You take an eighteenth-century book face and set it at a size no book would tolerate, which is broadly how a broadside gets made.
You want Baskerville's precision doing something impolite, the same instinct that put refined book faces on hardcore record sleeves throughout the 1990s.
transitional:refined: You are an editor at a magazine that still runs long features, and your Baskerville is set with the ligatures on and the widows hunted down.
You want the eighteenth century's manners without the museum, Fournier's proportions on a page designed for somebody who reads for two hours.
transitional:forward: You keep Baskerville's vertical stress and hand it to a rendering engine, which is roughly what happened to Times, and that did not end well.
Your picks want Enlightenment structure held to contemporary tolerances, the eighteenth century's logic applied to a screen it would have found appalling.
oldstyle:cool: Elzevir pocket editions sold old-style by the cartload to readers who never once bought one for the lettering, and you are buying on those same terms.
An archivist would recognise this, old-style proportions chosen because they still read at nine point and not because 1530 was a good year.
oldstyle:warm: You are in Claude Garamont's Paris with the light coming in sideways, choosing the angled stress and the ink that spreads a little into damp paper.
Your picks want Caslon on rough stock, the face that set the Declaration of Independence and roughly half the ale labels in England.
oldstyle:loud: You take Caslon and print it like a handbill nailed to a post, which is what Caslon actually spent most of its first century doing.
You want an old-style face with the press pushed too hard, ink filling the counters, far closer to a broadside than to a bible.
oldstyle:refined: You are setting a poetry list at a small press, Garamond with deep margins, and a decision about the em space you will defend for an hour.
You want Plantin's Antwerp workshop and its unfussy authority, old-style letters set by somebody who has never once been tempted by a display face.
oldstyle:forward: You are asking a 1530s punchcutter's alphabet to run inside an interface, which mostly works until somebody tries the italic at eleven point.
Your picks keep the angled stress and the small aperture and then look forward, which is the Sabon problem restated for a screen.
didone:cool: Imperial printing offices liked the didone because it looked like a decision that had already been taken, and nothing in this set invites the reader to argue with it.
Bodoni printed his own specimen book to argue that a page could be perfect, and your votes read it as an argument that a page could be correct.
didone:warm: You want Walbaum rather than Didot, the German didone with some blood left in it, which is the correct answer and not the fashionable one.
Your picks are Bodoni printed on paper soft enough to take the impression, warmth arriving through the press rather than through the drawing.
didone:loud: You take a fashion masthead face and blow it up until it stops being polite, which is precisely what a poster from 1968 wanted out of it.
You want a Didot used as a weapon, closer to a magazine cover screaming than to anything Firmin Didot did carefully in Paris.
didone:refined: You are Brodovitch at Harper's Bazaar, the type held at display size, white space treated as the most expensive material on the page.
You want Didot the way a fashion house wants it, deep margins and no clutter, with a nameplate nobody has been allowed to redraw in fifty years.
didone:forward: You want a didone to survive a screen, which is a hardware argument as much as a taste one, and you have clearly picked a side.
Your picks read as a didone drawn for a display that finally renders what the drawing intended, the nineteenth century's ambition given the resolution it wanted.
slab:cool: Figgins called it Antique and the fairgrounds took it away from him, and the reason it outlasted them is the reason you picked it, since a rectangle is hard to damage.
Clarendon was cut so a dictionary could mark a word without raising its voice, which is a functionary's reason to like a slab and looks like the only kind of reason on offer here.
slab:warm: Your picks want Clarendon on a jar label, the nineteenth-century Egyptian that came to mean warmth simply by outliving everything printed beside it.
You are in a country print shop in 1890, choosing the face that sold seed and horses and now sells coffee at a considerable markup.
slab:loud: You want the wanted poster, Figgins in 1815 selling ink by the acre, serifs squared off so nobody at the back can claim not to have seen it.
Your picks push Clarendon into the territory of a boxing bill, all shout and no small print, with no interest at all in a quiet room.
slab:refined: You want Memphis or Rockwell behaving in a catalogue, geometric slabs held at a size where the serifs read as structure rather than as costume.
You are the editor who sets decks in a slab and body in something else, a 1930s magazine move that still works and still annoys purists.
slab:forward: You want the Egyptian's rectangles as engineering, slabs treated like machined parts rather than like a nineteenth-century circus, which is roughly the Caecilia argument.
Your picks read as slab serifs for a control room, rectangles chosen because they hold at any size and never ask anyone for sympathy.

serif-brutal: You kept choosing serifs and then asking them to behave like poured concrete. That combination already has a name, and it is Clarendon on a demolition notice.
The category votes say serif and the moods say loading dock. Crouwel would have cut the serifs off and called it progress; you kept them and turned the volume up instead.

Nineteenth-century poster shops hit this wall and got out of it by fattening the serifs until they were structural rather than decorative. You have asked for the serif and the bruise in the same drawing, and that is a trade the wood-letter men only ever made in one direction.
sans-literary: You want a sans that reads like a novel, which is the problem Gill and later Frutiger spent whole careers on. The votes lean far enough away from serifs that there is not much left to hide behind.

The category votes went mostly sans and at least a third of the moods went bookish. That is a request for warmth without the parts that traditionally carry it, so the x-height is left doing work the serifs used to do.

The face that solved this is Optima, and Zapf solved it by smuggling broad-nib proportions in under a sans exterior. Short of that trick, the literary quality has to come out of the spacing and the proportions, which is a thinner rope than it sounds.
heavy-fine: Heavy and high-contrast at once is a fat didone, which is where display type goes to become unreadable below 60px. Bodoni's heirs have been fighting that for two centuries.
You asked for mass and then asked for hairlines inside it. The thin strokes go first at small sizes, and you will blame the printer when they do.

Poster Bodoni takes this trade honestly: below a certain size the hairlines stop pretending to be hairlines and get thickened until they survive the press. Your votes made no such concession, so the thin strokes are being asked to hold at a weight that will not protect them.
light-loud: A light stroke doing loud work is a strange assignment. Wood letter and the bold grotesques did their shouting entirely by ink coverage, and you have asked for the shout with the ink left out.
The weights you picked would disappear on a poster, and at least a third of your moods live nowhere else. Something has to give, and it is usually the weight.

A thin stroke can carry a loud face, but only at a metre and a half across a wall, where thin still means four millimetres of ink. At any size a screen can offer you, the loudness has to come from somewhere your weight votes refuse to fund.
wide-severe: Extended widths read as leisure, which is why they end up on car badges and wine labels. You then asked for clinical, and clinical does not sprawl.
Wide letters take up room that the severe moods would rather ration. Your picks want the authority of a Swiss grid and the footprint of a cinema marquee.

Wide and severe do meet, on instrument panels and record sleeves from about 1969, and they survive there by never setting more than three words at a time. The same drawing goes slack the moment it has to hold a caption.
narrow-warm: Condensed is an economy measure out of newspaper columns and price lists, and you have asked it to feel hospitable. Narrow type does not invite anyone to linger.
You compressed the letters and then asked them to be warm. The warmth will have to come from the terminals, because the counters have nowhere left to go.

Bell Gothic was condensed so a phone book would fit, and nobody in eighty years has described it as welcoming. Compression is a decision about cost, and you have asked the genome to make it read as generosity.
soft-cold: The softest endings on offer come out of the writing master's hand and the sign painter's brush, and neither of those is a clinical instrument. You voted at that end of the scale and then asked for a laboratory.

Rounded ends stay friendly at every size, so the severity would have to be carried by the skeleton instead, in flat sidewalls and tight fitting. Your terminal votes bought the opposite of that and kept buying it.

Cooper Black is the far end of this: the softness becomes the entire personality, and no amount of discipline elsewhere in the drawing pulls it back toward cold. Your terminal votes sit closer to that end than to anything with a laboratory in it.
hard-warm: You kept cutting the strokes off square and then asked the result to feel warm. Blunt terminals are the reason DIN reads as a road sign rather than as a letter.
Warmth in type usually arrives at the ends of the strokes, and you cut yours square. That leaves the counters to supply it, which gets you a face that is generous in the o and unhelpful in the l.

Flat terminals were an engineering convenience before anyone called them a style; they cut cleanly on a pantograph and they still read that way. What is left to make the face hospitable is wide counters and loose fitting, and neither of those is what your terminal votes were buying.
old-future: You picked eras that predate the light bulb and moods that postdate the keyboard. Every revival has this problem, and most solve it by lying about one of the two.
The Renaissance and the near-future are not natural partners, though phototypesetting had a good run pretending otherwise around 1972.

This is the Trajan-on-a-spaceship problem. It works when one era supplies the skeleton and the other supplies the surface, and it fails when both are asked to be the point, which is what your votes asked for.
split-category: Your votes divide near enough evenly between serifs and everything else, which is either open-mindedness or a refusal to decide. The genome cannot tell those apart.
You split the category axis about as evenly as it can be split. Roughly as many picks want the serif doing the talking as want it out of the way, and no single face settles that.

You voted for both sides of the oldest argument in type and left the genome to arbitrate. It arbitrates by averaging, and the average of a serif and a sans is a face neither camp asked for and neither will defend.
extreme-taste: You went looking for the ends of the axes far more often than the middle. Type drawn from extremes works at one size in one word, and stops being type the moment it has to hold a sentence.
Averaged across the axes you voted on, your picks sit a long way out from the centre. That is a display face, and it will be an awkward afternoon when somebody asks you for body copy.

Pushing the axes towards their limits is how display foundries have always made a living, and also why their catalogues run one weight deep. A drawing this far out has little room left to give you a second style.
middle-taste: Your picks average out very close to the centre of the axes, which is roughly how Times New Roman happened. Moderate is a real position; it just has a lot of prior occupants.
Whatever you did at the edges, the average landed in the middle. The result will be eminently usable and will be mistaken for a system font by anyone who is not looking hard.

Votes that average out this close to the centre produce the faces that ship with operating systems and get approved by committees. It will set anything you hand it, and you will not pick it out of a lineup a week later.
no-tension: There is no contradiction to point at. You picked a consistent set, which means either you knew what you wanted or the quiz never found the axis you would fight over.
Your picks agree with each other, which is rarer than it sounds. The risk in a set this consistent is not incoherence, it is that there is nothing in it pulling in a second direction.

Nothing in your votes argues with anything else, so there is no contradiction to report. Agreement this clean describes one face rather than a family, and it will keep describing one face however many names get hung on it.

decisive: Enough axes are pinned that the population will not wander far. Breed twice before you judge anything, because the first generation mostly repeats what you already told it.
You have given the genome enough constraints that it can stop guessing. Spend the wildcard slot generously; it is the only thing keeping the next four generations from looking alike.
Take the pinned axes into the pairing view and set the specimen text to something you actually have to publish. Constraints this firm flatter a headline and show their limits in a paragraph.
leaning: One or two axes are settled and the rest are still negotiable. Breed from here rather than returning to the quiz, because the loose axes resolve faster against real specimens than against paired questions.
You have a direction and not yet a specification. Keep two candidates per generation instead of one, and let the disagreement between them do the work.
The quiz found a preference before it found a face. Run a generation, keep the one that surprises you, and check whether the leaning still holds when the same drawing is set at 14px.
open: Nothing is pinned, so the first generation covers a lot of ground. Use that: cull hard and fast rather than trying to be fair to everything on screen.
You kept your options open, so the genome will too. The seed population is a spread by design, which makes the opening screen a survey rather than a shortlist.

No axis held still long enough to pin, so the search stays wide. Pick on instinct for a round or two, since the genome reads a fast cull exactly the way it reads a slow one and you will cover more of the space.

spurred.clause: spurs at the joins, a nod to nineteenth-century grotesques
spurred.reads: Small pointed nubs where strokes end, a Victorian habit

flared.label: flared
flared.clause: flared endings borrowed from carved Roman capitals
flared.reads: Ends widen slightly, like letters chiselled into stone

tapered.label: tapered
tapered.clause: tapered strokes that thin out the way a brush lifts
tapered.reads: Ends narrow to a point, as if the pen was lifting

rounded.label: rounded
rounded.clause: rounded ends in the VAG Rounded manner, friendly by construction
rounded.reads: Every stroke ends in a soft dome; nothing has a sharp edge

ball.label: ball
ball.clause: ball terminals, the little drops Baskerville hangs on an a
ball.reads: Strokes finish in a small round drop, a bookish flourish

small.label: small x-height
small.clause: a small x-height with the long ascenders that implies
small.reads: Lowercase letters sit low, so the tall ones stand out

modest.label: modest x-height
modest.clause: a modest x-height in the old-style habit, Garamond's proportion
modest.reads: Slightly small lowercase, which gives the line an even, quiet texture

normal.label: normal x-height
normal.clause: a normal x-height, the proportion nobody argues about
normal.reads: Lowercase sits where you expect it, neither cramped nor looming

large.label: large x-height
large.clause: a large x-height that buys legibility at small sizes
large.reads: Lowercase letters run tall, so text holds up when set small

very large.label: very large x-height
very large.clause: a very large x-height, ascenders barely clearing the lowercase
very large.reads: Lowercase nearly as tall as the capitals; the line looks dense

razor-sharp.label: razor corners
razor-sharp.clause: corners left razor sharp, the drawing as the Bézier handles delivered it
razor-sharp.reads: Every join comes to a hard point, with nothing rounded off

crisp.label: crisp corners
crisp.clause: crisp joins with about as much rounding as ink gain used to add
crisp.reads: Angles read sharp, though the corners are not quite surgical up close

softened.label: softened corners
softened.clause: corners taken down the way a face comes back from newsprint
softened.reads: Angles are visibly eased, so the letters look worn in rather than filed

rounded.label: rounded corners
rounded.clause: corners turned to one consistent radius, the router-bit finish of moulded lettering
rounded.reads: Each angle is a small curve; the edges look tumbled instead of cut

pillowy.label: pillowy corners
pillowy.clause: a radius pushed well past comfort, in the bubble-lettering habit of 1972
pillowy.reads: Corners so round the letters look inflated, nearer a logo than a text face

clean.label: clean
clean.clause: a clean outline with no surface at all, drawn for vector and vinyl
clean.reads: Smooth edges, exactly as the drawing program left them

lightly inked.label: lightly inked
lightly inked.clause: a light ink gain along the edge, the weight letterpress hands back
lightly inked.reads: Strokes thicken very slightly, as if pressed into damp paper

slightly rough.label: slightly rough
slightly rough.clause: an outline roughened just enough to look printed rather than plotted
slightly rough.reads: Small irregularities along the stems, obvious at poster size and invisible in text

engraved.label: engraved
engraved.clause: an engraved surface with the burin lines still sitting in the stems, banknote practice
engraved.reads: Fine cut lines inside the strokes, the look of a share certificate

brush-drawn.label: brush-drawn
brush-drawn.clause: a brush-drawn edge that keeps the bristle marks, sign painter rather than punchcutter
brush-drawn.reads: Strokes swell and go dry the way a loaded brush does across a board

eroded.label: eroded
eroded.clause: an eroded outline, type that has been left out in the weather
eroded.reads: Bitten, pitted edges; some counters start closing where the ink has eaten in

stencil-cut.label: stencil-cut
stencil-cut.clause: a stencil cut with the bridges left in, out of the crate-and-airfield tradition
stencil-cut.reads: Gaps break the strokes where a stencil needs a bridge, so the o comes apart

pixel-stepped.label: pixel-stepped
pixel-stepped.clause: a pixel-stepped outline that admits its grid, screen-font logic blown up to poster size
pixel-stepped.reads: Curves climb in visible steps, as though drawn on a coarse grid

editorial.label: editorial
editorial.clause: an editorial voice, drawn to be read on deadline
editorial.reads: Feels like a magazine page, built to carry a headline and a story

brutalist.label: brutalist
brutalist.clause: a brutalist streak, nearer a poured concrete signboard than a typeface with manners
brutalist.reads: Heavy and plain, with every refinement stripped out on purpose

warm.label: warm
warm.clause: a warmth carried in the curves, the way Sabon stays friendly with no flourishes at all
warm.reads: Softer shapes that feel written by a person rather than machined

clinical.label: clinical
clinical.clause: a clinical evenness, the register of a lab label
clinical.reads: Cool and exact, the tone of instructions you are meant to follow

nostalgic.label: nostalgic
nostalgic.clause: a nostalgia for the shopfront lettering nobody repaints
nostalgic.reads: Looks like something remembered from an older sign or record sleeve

futuristic.label: futuristic
futuristic.clause: a futurism that dates itself the moment it lands
futuristic.reads: Forward-looking shapes, the kind every decade thinks it invented

literary.label: literary
literary.clause: a literary temperament that assumes long paragraphs
literary.reads: Made for sustained reading, the tone of a printed book

industrial.label: industrial
industrial.clause: an industrial register borrowed from stencilled crate lettering
industrial.reads: Built for signs on machinery rather than for pages

playful.label: playful
playful.clause: a playfulness that stops just short of a cartoon
playful.reads: Loose and cheerful, more at home on a toy box than a contract

severe.label: severe
severe.clause: a severity in the DIN register, drawn to instruct rather than to please
severe.reads: Stern and unfriendly on purpose, with nothing soft to hold onto

elegant.label: elegant
elegant.clause: an elegance that depends on generous margins
elegant.reads: Refined and slightly formal, the look of an invitation

utilitarian.label: utilitarian
utilitarian.clause: a utilitarian bias, drawn for the job and looked at afterwards
utilitarian.reads: Plain and practical; it wants to be useful before it is admired

psychedelic.label: psychedelic
psychedelic.clause: a psychedelic streak out of the Fillmore poster shop
psychedelic.reads: Letters bend and crowd each other, like a 1967 concert poster

ecclesiastical.label: ecclesiastical
ecclesiastical.clause: an ecclesiastical air, blackletter without the blackletter
ecclesiastical.reads: Solemn and churchy, the tone of an inscription or a hymnal

botanical.label: botanical
botanical.clause: a botanical line, closer to a stem than a girder
botanical.reads: Growing, organic curves, the feel of a plant guide or apothecary label

mechanical.label: mechanical
mechanical.clause: a mechanical construction you could redraw with a compass
mechanical.reads: Built from repeated parts, as if assembled rather than drawn

15th-century humanist.label: early renaissance
15th-century humanist.clause: a fifteenth-century hand, Jenson's Venice by way of the pen
15th-century humanist.reads: The shapes of the first printed books, still close to handwriting

18th-century enlightenment.label: enlightenment
18th-century enlightenment.clause: an eighteenth-century rationalism, Baskerville arguing with the pen
18th-century enlightenment.reads: Cooler and more even than handwriting, the age of the printed page

19th-century industrial.label: industrial century
19th-century industrial.clause: the nineteenth century's poster trade, wood type and volume
19th-century industrial.reads: Loud commercial lettering from the age of playbills and shopfronts

1920s Bauhaus.label: bauhaus
1920s Bauhaus.reads: Letters reduced to circles and straight lines on principle

1950s Swiss.label: swiss modern
1950s Swiss.clause: the Swiss fifties, a grid and no adjectives
1950s Swiss.reads: Neutral, tightly spaced and orderly, the look of postwar Zurich

1970s phototypesetting.label: phototype era
1970s phototypesetting.clause: the phototype seventies, letters tight enough to touch
1970s phototypesetting.reads: Close-set, curvy lettering from the era of film and airbrush

1990s digital.label: early digital
1990s digital.clause: the nineties, when Emigre made bad screens a style
1990s digital.reads: Early computer type, when low resolution shaped how letters were drawn

contemporary.label: contemporary
contemporary.clause: a contemporary drawing, variable axes and no nostalgia
contemporary.reads: Current practice: flexible, made for screens and print at once

speculative near-future.label: near-future
speculative near-future.clause: a near-future guess, the kind film titles make
speculative near-future.reads: Shapes that read as tomorrow, borrowed from science fiction more than research

verdicts.geometric:cool: You make taste look like arithmetic.
verdicts.geometric:warm: Your sentimentality arrives on a grid.
verdicts.geometric:loud: You bring a ruler to a riot.
verdicts.geometric:refined: Precision is how you show off.
verdicts.geometric:forward: You believe the future has one shape.
verdicts.neogrotesque:cool: You treat neutrality as a moral position.
verdicts.neogrotesque:warm: You expect the exit sign to like you.
verdicts.neogrotesque:loud: You hand the megaphone to the quietest person.
verdicts.neogrotesque:refined: You could not be accused of anything here.
verdicts.neogrotesque:forward: You picture the future and it is beige.
verdicts.grotesque:cool: You trust anything that predates good taste.
verdicts.grotesque:warm: You find plain speech endearing, which it is not.
verdicts.grotesque:loud: You back the letters that pay rent.
verdicts.grotesque:refined: You have expensive taste in ordinary things.
verdicts.grotesque:forward: You strip the provenance off it.
verdicts.humanist-sans:cool: Who drew it is not your concern.
verdicts.humanist-sans:warm: You mistrust an alphabet that never wavers.
verdicts.humanist-sans:loud: Everything you like is trying to sell something.
verdicts.humanist-sans:refined: You think a sans can be well-read.
verdicts.humanist-sans:forward: You insist on a pulse in the machinery.
verdicts.flared:cool: You approve of history when it stays quiet.
verdicts.flared:warm: You would call this restraint; it is longing.
verdicts.flared:loud: You use the sacred to push people around.
verdicts.flared:refined: You want the applause to be inaudible.
verdicts.wedge:cool: You like your authority delivered in a memo.
verdicts.wedge:warm: You take your comfort in granite.
verdicts.wedge:loud: You point this at somebody in particular.
verdicts.wedge:refined: Your taste comes with a marble floor.
verdicts.wedge:forward: You give the future something to obey.
verdicts.humanist-serif:cool: You are unmoved by the things you love.
verdicts.humanist-serif:refined: You are impossible to buy books for.
verdicts.humanist-serif:forward: You assume the old drawing survives translation.
verdicts.transitional:cool: You promote the compromise to a principle.
verdicts.transitional:warm: You soften for anything with decent manners.
verdicts.transitional:loud: You recruit reason for something unreasonable.
verdicts.transitional:refined: Nobody has ever seen you call it finished.
verdicts.transitional:forward: Your faith in hardware is touching.
verdicts.oldstyle:cool: You inherit the method and skip the myth.
verdicts.oldstyle:loud: Good breeding means nothing to you.
verdicts.oldstyle:refined: Your standards have never been profitable.
verdicts.oldstyle:forward: You put an antique on the payroll.
verdicts.didone:cool: You enjoy being slightly punished by a page.
verdicts.didone:warm: You look for tenderness in a guillotine.
verdicts.didone:loud: You would rather be seen than read.
verdicts.didone:refined: You perform wealth you may not have.
verdicts.didone:forward: Somewhere there is a monitor worthy of you.
verdicts.slab:warm: You feel safest around solid furniture.
verdicts.slab:loud: You are not asking; you are announcing.
verdicts.slab:refined: You dress a labourer for dinner.
verdicts.slab:forward: You want a typeface with a warranty.
